interpretation: Single fine crack. Hairline cracks usually form when an egg strikes a hard surface, and early-lay shells are normally strong, so a handling or equipment impact is the most likely cause.
suggested_actions: Walk the egg route: nest mats, belt transitions and trolley or tray surfaces; collect at least 4 times a day; train staff to place eggs gently in trays. Confirm the diet has moved from pre-breeder to Breeder 1 (about 3.0% calcium).
evidence: Hairline cracks from contact with inflexible surfaces (Gupta 2008, cited in Poultry Science 2023 study on sealing cracked hatching eggs); Ross 308 PS Breeder 1 calcium 3.00%.

interpretation: Single fine crack at peak or post-peak lay. Impact is still the main trigger, but high egg output and a falling shell-to-egg ratio make shells easier to crack.
suggested_actions: Fix impact points on the egg route first (nest mats, belt speed, transfer points, collection at least 4 times a day). Check diet calcium matches Breeder 2 (about 3.2%), and check house temperature on hot afternoons.
evidence: Gupta 2008, cited in Poultry Science 2023 cracked hatching egg study; Ross 308 PS Breeder 2 calcium 3.20%; shell thickness declines as egg size rises (Oliveira et al. 2026).

interpretation: Single fine crack in an older flock. Calcium absorption and shell deposition fall with age, so a thinner shell is now as likely a cause as the impact itself.
suggested_actions: Check diet calcium matches Breeder 3 (about 3.4%); add coarse limestone (2-4 mm) or oyster shell in the late afternoon; check vitamin D3 supply; keep eggs cool and handle them gently, as thinner shells crack at lower forces.
evidence: Ross 308 PS Breeder 3 calcium 3.40%; Ross Note on egg shell quality (afternoon coarse calcium for older flocks); peak to late lay shell thickness -3%, strength up to -30% (BMC Genomics 2026).

interpretation: Cracks radiating from one point show a point impact, most often from eggs colliding. With normally strong early-lay shells, a mechanical cause is very likely.
suggested_actions: Look for egg-to-egg collisions: increase collection frequency so eggs do not pile up on the belt, check belt start/stop speed and the end of the belt, and avoid stacking or knocking trays.
evidence: Star cracks linked to egg collisions (Gupta 2008, cited in Poultry Science 2023 study on sealing cracked hatching eggs); shell damage in nests, collection and storage (Pilotto et al. 2015, cited in the same study).

interpretation: Point-impact crack during peak lay. More eggs on the belt means more collisions, so handling and equipment are the main cause.
suggested_actions: Increase collection frequency during peak lay, check belt speed and transfer points, and inspect nest boxes for hard edges. Keep diet calcium at the Breeder 2 level (about 3.2%).
evidence: Gupta 2008, cited in Poultry Science 2023 cracked hatching egg study; Ross 308 PS Breeder 2 calcium 3.20%.

interpretation: Point-impact crack in an older flock. The impact is still the main cause, but thinner late-lay shells break under smaller knocks.
suggested_actions: Fix collision points on the belt and in handling first; then check Breeder 3 calcium (about 3.4%) and afternoon coarse calcium, because weaker shells amplify impact damage.
evidence: Gupta 2008, cited in Poultry Science 2023 cracked hatching egg study; Ross 308 PS Breeder 3 calcium 3.40%; age-related decline in shell strength (BMC Genomics 2026).

interpretation: Several connected fine cracks from one event suggest the shell could not spread the load. In a young flock this points to a weak shell (for example an incomplete switch to breeder feed or heat stress) together with handling.
suggested_actions: Confirm the flock moved to Breeder 1 feed (about 3.0% calcium) on time and is eating its full allocation; check house temperature and cooling, as panting above about 25 C thins shells; also review handling.
evidence: Ross 308 PS pre-breeder 1.20% vs Breeder 1 3.00% calcium; heat stress and respiratory alkalosis reduce shell calcium carbonate (Barrett et al. 2019, Poultry Science; MDPI Animals 2024 heat stress study).

interpretation: Widespread fine cracking at peak or post-peak lay suggests calcium supply or shell formation is not keeping up with high egg output.
suggested_actions: Check diet calcium and available phosphorus against Breeder 2 (about 3.2% Ca, 0.34% available P) and that hens reach about 5 g calcium per day; check vitamin D3; check house temperature, water intake and water salinity; ask a vet to rule out disease if cracking rises suddenly.
evidence: Ross 308 PS peak calcium allocation about 5.0 g/bird/day; heat stress effects (Barrett et al. 2019); water salinity and drugs affect shell quality (Gupta, The Poultry Site 2019).

interpretation: Widespread fine cracking in an older flock strongly suggests age-related shell weakness: calcium absorption and shell gland activity decline after peak lay.
suggested_actions: Move to Breeder 3 calcium (about 3.4%); add 2-4 mm limestone or oyster shell in the late afternoon (about 2 g per bird); check vitamin D3; reduce heat stress; increase shell quality checks and consider flock age in replacement planning.
evidence: Ross 308 PS Breeder 3 calcium 3.40%; Ross Note on egg shell quality (coarse calcium for older breeders); shell gland ageing (BMC Genomics 2026).
